item.text: I’ll look through the material folder and use your work and personality to shape the concept, then map out the full experience before any building starts.

item.aggregated_output:
Some notes from me (Ines)

Pictures I have:
- about 60 photos of dishes and the jar wall, taken by Priya Nair for the
  restaurant's website
- my own phone photos of the larder, labels and all
- scans of all four issues of Brine (drawings by my friend Olu)
- a photo of my grandmother's ogiri pot

Things people ask me about: the jar wall, the koji room (it is a cupboard),
the staff meal, and the workshops I run on the first Monday of the month.

I took over the kitchen in September 2022.

Books that got me here: The Art of Fermentation by Sandor Katz, and Wild
Fermentation. And my grandmother, who never measured anything.
(Saved from LinkedIn as text, October 2026)

Ines Okafor
Head Chef at Saltmarsh. Fermentation, whole-vegetable cooking, apprentices.
Leeds, England, United Kingdom

ABOUT
I cook at Saltmarsh, a 40-seat restaurant in Leeds. Most of what I care about
happens before service: what we do with the trim, the whey, the stems and the
bones. We have a wall of jars and a prep list that is longer than the menu.
I run our apprentice programme and write a small zine about preserving,
called Brine.

EXPERIENCE

Head Chef, Saltmarsh, Leeds
Mar 2022 to present
- A menu that changes every week
- Cut kitchen food waste from 14 kg to 5 kg a week
- Built the larder: 40+ ferments, vinegars and garums on rotation
- Two apprentices a year since 2023

Sous Chef, The Corn Exchange Kitchen, Leeds
Jun 2019 to Feb 2022
- Ran the pass on a 90-cover service
- Took over ordering and brought the supplier list from 31 to 12

Chef de Partie, Brassica, Manchester
Sep 2016 to May 2019
- Larder and garnish, then sauce

Fjaerland Fermentation Lab, Norway
Jan 2018 to Mar 2018

EDUCATION
Leeds Kitchen College. Diploma in Professional Cookery, 2014 to 2016

VOLUNTEERING
Sunday Pot, Leeds. Co-founder. 2021 to present
A hot meal every Sunday at St Aidan's hall, cooked from what restaurants in
the city have left over.

PUBLICATIONS
Brine. A zine about preserving. Four issues, 2022 to 2025.

RECOMMENDATIONS
Callum Reyes, owner of Saltmarsh:
"Ines turned our bins into a larder. The best thing on the menu most weeks
started as something we used to throw away."

item.text:
The strongest thread is what happens before service: the jars, the scraps becoming ingredients, the apprentices, and Brine. I’m shaping the site around an unfolding larder, with 3D revealing that work as you scroll.

The folder contains two text files describing your images, rather than the images themselves. There’s also a date to reconcile: your notes say you took over the kitchen in September 2022, while LinkedIn lists March 2022.

The idea is **“Before service” — a portfolio built around your living larder.** Visitors meet Ines Okafor through the things you keep, transform, cook and teach: the jar wall, a finished dish, an apprentice’s work, a page of *Brine*.

That gives the 3D and movement a purpose. Scrolling reveals how your work develops over time, from overlooked ingredient to something worth serving.

This plan is based on the two text files in `material`. They describe your photographs and scans; the visual direction below is provisional until those assets can be reviewed. Nothing has been built.

**The site’s job.** Establish your identity as a chef, show the substance behind your practice, and help people find the right next step: visit Saltmarsh, attend a workshop, explore apprenticeships, or contact you about work. Saltmarsh anchors the story, while *Brine*, Sunday Pot and your teaching make this unmistakably your portfolio.

**The scroll, from top to bottom**

1. **Arrive at the larder.**

   A large, quietly lit 3D arrangement of a few jars sits alongside direct introductory copy:

   > Ines Okafor  
   > Head chef, Saltmarsh, Leeds.  
   > Most of my work happens before service.

   The jars should be based on your actual vessels and labels. Uneven tape, handwriting and cloudy contents provide the character; the treatment should feel like a working kitchen.

   As the visitor begins scrolling, the viewpoint moves gently toward one label. The introduction stays readable independently of the scene. A visible “Explore the work” link provides a straightforward way onward.

2. **Open the working larder.**

   The dimensional scene settles into a flat editorial layout: photographs, labels and short ingredient stories. This is the transition from atmosphere to evidence.

   Feature three actual examples from your current larder. Each follows the same useful sequence: **what came into the kitchen → what you did with it → where it ended up**. The examples need your input; I would not invent fermentation methods or durations from the notes.

   Include the scale of the practice here: **40+ ferments, vinegars and garums on rotation**, and kitchen food waste reduced **from 14 kg to 5 kg a week**. Date and contextualise those figures before publication.

   A small photograph captioned “The koji room. It’s a cupboard.” would bring your voice into the page without forcing a joke.

3. **See what reaches the plate.**

   Move into generous food photography: three selected dishes, each paired with a process or larder detail. This section must show that the thinking produces food people want to eat.

   On desktop, a process image can remain in place briefly while its dish and explanation move alongside it. Captions explain the relevant ingredient and decision in a few lines.

   Present these as selected dishes, with dates or seasons where available. Your weekly-changing menu belongs on Saltmarsh’s site; this portfolio should not imply these dishes are available tonight.

4. **Meet the kitchen around the food.**

   The visual rhythm becomes warmer and more documentary: staff meal, prep, teaching, and hands at work, if suitable photographs exist.

   Introduce the apprentice programme—two apprentices a year since 2023—and what you want people to learn in your kitchen. Place the first-Monday workshops here, with a short explanation of what participants can expect.

   Give Sunday Pot its own clear passage: the hot meal every Sunday at St Aidan’s hall, cooked from restaurant surplus. It connects your resourcefulness to people beyond the restaurant.

   Movement becomes minimal here. The people and words deserve the attention.

5. **Read *Brine*.**

   Four issues form a loose stack on a paper-coloured background. As this section enters view, the covers separate slightly, making each issue available to open.

   Selecting an issue opens a readable page with its cover, a brief introduction, selected spreads and an accessible text version. Offer a downloadable PDF if the scans and permissions support it. Avoid making a simulated page-turn animation the only way to read.

   Olu’s drawings can give this section a visual identity that could only come from your work. Credit Olu visibly.

6. **Trace where it began.**

   Use the photograph of your grandmother’s ogiri pot as the focal point for a short personal passage, written or approved by you. Your note that she “never measured anything” is a strong starting point; the site should leave room for the actual story behind it.

   Follow with a compact career timeline: training in Leeds, Brassica, the Norway lab, The Corn Exchange Kitchen, and Saltmarsh. Confirm how the Norway placement overlapped with Brassica and reconcile the March/September 2022 dates before publishing.

   The books that influenced you can appear as a small reading note alongside your grandmother’s influence.

7. **Leave with an invitation.**

   Finish with Callum Reyes’s recommendation:

   > “Ines turned our bins into a larder. The best thing on the menu most weeks started as something we used to throw away.”

   Then offer clearly named routes: **Workshops**, **Apprenticeships**, **Contact Ines**, and **Visit Saltmarsh**. Only show applications or bookings as open when that is confirmed.

   A small jar-label motif closes the page without another large animation.

**The visual language.** Use warm paper (`#F2EBDD`), near-black ink (`#252722`), muted larder green (`#4E5B45`) and a restrained brine amber (`#A45A2A`). Paper and ink carry the reading experience; green and amber identify links, labels and small accents. Check final text combinations for accessible contrast.

Set headlines in **Newsreader**, with its literary, slightly irregular character, and body copy in **Public Sans** for clarity. Small factual labels can use the sans serif with tabular numerals. Actual handwriting should come from your labels and scans, rather than a handwriting font.

Pair carefully shot dishes with your phone photographs of the larder. That difference in polish tells a useful story. Keep texture subtle and preserve clean reading surfaces. Credit Priya Nair’s photography wherever appropriate.

**How the motion should feel.** Slow, tactile and limited to meaningful transitions: approaching a jar, connecting a process to a dish, separating the zine covers. The opening is the main 3D moment. Standard scrolling, visible navigation and ordinary links remain available throughout. No loading sequence before your name appears, custom cursor, or scroll hijacking.

**On a phone.** Use a single-column story with food and labels large enough to inspect. Start with a lightweight still of the jar composition; add motion only where the device can handle it comfortably. Turn desktop image pairings into sequential process-and-result cards. Show *Brine* covers as a simple grid with tap-to-read pages. Avoid horizontal scroll sections and hover-dependent information.

Reduced-motion mode gets still compositions and simple transitions. The complete site must remain readable and navigable without WebGL, using keyboard controls and assistive technology.

**What else the site needs.**

- **A small, maintainable structure:** one main story page, individual *Brine* pages, workshop information, and contact details. Add separate work stories only when there is enough material to justify them.
- **An asset and permissions check:** select from the photographs you describe; confirm personal-site use with Priya, use of Olu’s drawings, and consent for identifiable staff or apprentices.
- **A short content session with you:** three ingredient stories, three dishes, your grandmother’s pot story, your teaching approach, and current contact and booking routes.
- **Fast delivery:** responsive images, lazy-loaded scans, and deferred 3D. Your name, introduction and navigation should appear immediately.
- **Findability and upkeep:** descriptive page titles, social previews, image descriptions, working links, and an easy way to update workshops, issues and availability. A contact form, if needed, should have spam protection and a concise privacy notice.

The distinctive element is already in your material: a practice built around what other kitchens might discard. The design should make visitors curious enough to look closely—and give them real work to discover when they do.
